title: AI for Social Media
description: Why generated posts read as generated, how writing for a feed differs from writing for a page, why the comment section is the most valuable thing you produce, and what actually differs between platforms.

modules.title: The Course
modules.description: Four lessons on social text that people stop for.

lessons.title: Why Generated Posts Read as Generated

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Generated social posts have a recognisable shape: a rhetorical question, three tidy points, a summarising line, and a call to engage. Readers scroll past all of it at identical speed.

The problem is not quality. It is that the post could have been written by anyone about anything.

blocks.heading: Feeds Reward Specificity, Not Polish
blocks.bodyHtml:
«Consistency is key to growing your audience. Here are three tips…»

«I posted every day for six weeks and got nothing. Week seven I changed one thing — the first line — and the same content did four times the reach.»

The second is a story with a number in it. The first is advice that everyone has already read.

blocks.text: Nobody stops scrolling for something they could have predicted.

blocks.heading: Four Markers Readers Recognise
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The rhetorical opener — «Ever wondered why…?»
  • Exactly three tidy points, all the same length
  • A summarising final line that adds nothing
  • «What do you think? Comment below»

Removing all four leaves a shorter post that has to contain something real, which is the entire fix.

blocks.question: Which post opening is most likely to stop someone scrolling?

options.label: Ever wondered why some businesses grow faster than others do?
We lost two customers last month for the same avoidable reason.
Here are five proven strategies for improving your online presence.
Consistency and quality are the foundation of every strong brand.

blocks.successBody: A specific admission with a number is something only this business could post, and it promises information the reader does not already have. The other three are recognisable as the opening of a post they have read many times.
blocks.wrongHint: Ask which line could only have been written by someone with an actual experience to report.

blocks.heading: Supply the Raw Material
blocks.bodyHtml:
The useful split is the same as everywhere else: you supply what happened, it handles the arrangement.

A post generated from «write about customer service» is empty. A post generated from «a customer complained about X, we changed Y, here is what happened» is worth reading, and the difference took you thirty seconds to type.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Write down three things that actually happened in your work this month.
Pick the one with a number attached.
Draft a post from that alone, with no advice in it.
Compare it to a post generated from the topic without the story.

blocks.heading: Advice Is the Weakest Format
blocks.bodyHtml:
Advice posts are the easiest to generate and the most ignored, because everyone is producing them.

What is scarce is what happened to you: the number, the mistake, the thing that did not work. That material cannot be generated, and it is the only durable advantage anyone has in a feed.

blocks.body: Generated posts read as generated because they could have been written by anyone. Cut the rhetorical opener, the three tidy points, the summarising line and the engagement bait — then build posts from things that actually happened, with numbers, rather than from topics.

lessons.title: Writing for a Feed, Not a Page

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
A feed is not a page. The reader is moving, the preview is cut off after two lines, and nothing is guaranteed to be read in order.

Most weak posts are well-written pages published in the wrong place.

blocks.heading: The Preview Is the Whole Post
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most platforms show one or two lines before «more». That fragment decides everything else.

«I've been thinking a lot recently about how small businesses approach their pricing, and I wanted to share some thoughts…»

«We raised our prices 20% and lost one customer out of forty.»

The first spends the preview announcing that a post exists. The second spends it saying something.

blocks.text: The first two lines are not an introduction. They are the advert for the rest.

blocks.heading: Four Rules for Feed Text
blocks.bodyHtml:
• No warm-up — start inside the idea
  • Line breaks often — dense blocks are skipped on a phone
  • One idea per post — a second idea halves both
  • End on a line worth quoting, not a question

These are formatting rules, not writing rules, which is why they are easy to apply and easy to forget.

blocks.question: Your posts get impressions but very few people expand them. What should you change?

options.label: The posting time, so they appear when your audience is most active.
The first two lines, since that fragment is all most people ever see.
The length, making each post shorter so it fits without expanding.
The hashtags, so the posts reach a more relevant set of readers.

blocks.successBody: Impressions without expansion means the post was shown and the preview did not earn a click. That is the first two lines and nothing else — timing and hashtags affect whether it appears at all.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about which stage the reader actually stops at, and what they saw at that moment.

blocks.heading: Write the Ending Before the Middle
blocks.bodyHtml:
Decide the one line you want remembered, then write towards it. Posts that end on a question usually end on the weakest sentence in them.

A quotable closing line is also what gets screenshotted and shared, which no engagement prompt has ever achieved.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take three of your posts and read only the first two lines of each.
Rewrite one so the first line contains the actual point.
Add line breaks so no block exceeds three lines on a phone.
Replace the closing question with a line you would want quoted.

blocks.heading: Read It on a Phone
blocks.bodyHtml:
Almost everything is read on a phone and almost everything is written on a desktop. A paragraph that looks tidy on a laptop is a wall of text on a screen half the width.

Preview every post on your phone before posting. It takes ten seconds and changes what you publish.

blocks.body: A feed is not a page: the preview is the whole advert, so start inside the idea rather than warming up. Break lines often, keep one idea per post, end on a quotable line rather than a question, and check every post on a phone before it goes out.

lessons.title: The Comment Section Is the Product

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Most people treat comments as a metric. They are actually the most useful thing social media produces, and the part that generated content handles worst.

What people say back is unfiltered market research that no survey would get you.

blocks.heading: Reply Like a Person
blocks.bodyHtml:
Generated replies are instantly recognisable: warm, generic and slightly too long.

«Thank you so much for your thoughtful comment! We really appreciate your support.»

«That's the bit we got wrong for two years. What finally fixed it was doing the opposite.»

The second continues a conversation. The first ends one politely.

blocks.text: A generic reply is worse than no reply — it tells the commenter nobody was there.

blocks.heading: Three Things Comments Give You
blocks.bodyHtml:
• The objection you had not thought of — free, and honest
  • The phrasing your customers use — better than any wording you invent
  • Your next five posts — every question is a post

The third is the one people miss. A recurring question in your comments is a post that is guaranteed to land.

blocks.question: Someone leaves a sceptical comment disagreeing with your post. What is the best response?

options.label: Ignore it — arguing in public rarely reflects well on a business.
Answer the substance directly and agree with whatever part is fair.
Reply privately so the disagreement is not visible to other readers.
Thank them for the perspective without engaging with the argument.

blocks.successBody: Everyone else reading is watching how you handle disagreement, and a direct answer that concedes a fair point builds more trust than the original post did. Deflection is visible and reads as having no answer.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what the silent readers learn from each of these responses.

blocks.heading: Harvest Them Monthly
blocks.bodyHtml:
Once a month, gather every question and objection from your comments and messages, and group them.

That list is your content plan, your sales page objections and your product feedback simultaneously — and it costs nothing but the reading.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Collect every question from your last month of comments.
Group them and find the one that keeps returning.
Write that post using the commenter's own wording.
Reply to three old comments you never answered.

blocks.heading: Never Automate the Reply
blocks.bodyHtml:
This is the one place to keep entirely human. An auto-reply in a comment section is visible to everyone, not just the person who wrote it, and it signals precisely what you would not want to signal.

Draft with a tool if you like. Send as yourself, and read every word first.

blocks.body: Comments are the most useful output of social media: the objections you missed, your customers' own phrasing, and your next five posts. Answer disagreement directly and concede what is fair, harvest questions monthly, and never automate a public reply.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.bodyHtml:
Advice about platforms is mostly folklore: post at this hour, use this many hashtags, the algorithm favours that. Most of it is stale within a season.

A few differences are structural, and those are worth knowing because they do not change.

blocks.heading: Three Structural Differences
blocks.bodyHtml:
• Who sees it — your followers, or people who do not know you
  • How long it lives — hours, or months of search traffic
  • What the format rewards — text, image, video, or discussion

Everything else — timing, hashtags, posting frequency — is tuning. These three decide whether a piece of content belongs there at all.

blocks.text: Ask what a platform rewards structurally, not what its algorithm reportedly likes this month.

blocks.heading: Reshape, Do Not Repost
blocks.bodyHtml:
Writing one post and pasting the identical text everywhere.

Taking one idea and rebuilding it: a story where discussion is rewarded, a single image where scanning is, a short video where watching is.

Same idea, three shapes, thirty minutes. Identical text in three places performs badly in at least two of them.

blocks.question: You have one good idea. How should it be published across platforms?

options.label: Post the same text everywhere so the message stays perfectly consistent.
Rebuild it in the format each platform rewards, keeping the same idea.
Choose the single platform that performs best and publish only there.
Post it first where it works best, then repost elsewhere a week later.

blocks.successBody: The idea travels; the format does not. Rebuilding takes minutes and works everywhere, while identical text is optimised for whichever platform you wrote it for and mediocre on the rest.
blocks.wrongHint: Think about what actually needs to change between platforms — the idea, or the shape it takes?

blocks.heading: Use Tools for the Reshaping
blocks.bodyHtml:
This is exactly the repetitive work worth handing over: «here is the post, rewrite it as a short video script» or «as a single-image caption of under forty words».

You keep the idea and the specifics; it handles the shape. That is thirty minutes saved per idea, every time.

blocks.heading: Try
items: Take one recent post and identify which format its platform rewards.
Rebuild the same idea for a second platform in a different shape.
Publish both and compare which parts of the idea survived.
Note which reshaping took longest — automate that one next time.

blocks.heading: Pick Two, Not Five
blocks.bodyHtml:
Being present everywhere with weak content beats being absent, but it loses badly to being good in two places.

Choose the two where your buyers actually are, do those properly, and ignore the rest until the first two are working.

blocks.body: Only three things differ structurally: who sees it, how long it lives, and what format it rewards. Everything else is tuning. Rebuild one idea into the shape each platform rewards rather than reposting identical text — and do two platforms well instead of five badly.
